Socrates, again

  • Premises

    • P1: all men are mortal,
    • P2: Socrates is a man,

  • Conclusion

    then Socrates is mortal.

Example

  • Premises

    • P1: if the sum of the digits of a whole number is a multiple of \(3\), then the number is divisible by \(3\)
    • P2: if the last digit of a whole number is a \(5\) or a \(0\), then the number is divisible by \(5\).

  • Conclusion

    The number \(2715\) is divisible by both \(3\) and \(5\).

Terminology

  • Premise: a statement assumed (or previously proved) true,

  • Conclusion: logical result of two or more premises.

  • Valid: conclusion follows from premises

    it is impossible for premises to be true and conclusion to be false

  • Invalid: conclusion does not follow from premises.

  • Sound: valid and all premises are true.

  • Unsound: may be valid, but one or more premises may be false or faulty.

Example: invalid

  • Premises

    • P1: Plato is a great thinker,
    • P2: Plato is a man,

  • Conclusion

    it follows that all humans are great thinkers.

  • P1 and P2 only give information about Plato,

  • we cannot generalise to all humans.

EXample: invalid

  • Premises

    • P1: if the sum of the digits of a whole number is a multiple of \(3\), then the number is divisible by \(3\)
    • P2: if the last digit of a whole number is a \(5\) or a \(0\), then the number is divisible by \(5\).

  • Conclusion

    The number \(2710\) is divisible by both \(3\) and \(5\).

  • P2 can be applied because the last digit is \(0\),

  • but P1 does not apply because \(2 + 7 + 1 + 0 = 10\) is not a multiple of \(3\).

Example: valid but unsound

  • Premises

    • P1: all men are mortal,
    • P2: Socrates is a man,

  • Conclusion

    then Socrates is mortal.

  • One might argue that Socrates is a Lizard person, so P1 is false.

Example: valid but unsound

  • Premises

    • P1: there are no even prime numbers.

  • Conclusion

    then \(2\), being even, is not a prime number.

  • \(2\), divisible by only \(1\) and itself, is clearly even and a prime number, so P1 is false.

Checking Deductive Logic

Mathematical proofs and programming

  • Mathematical proofs rely on deductive logic,

  • and, possibly more relevant, so does programming.

    • We can say a program is valid if it runs without crashing.

    • But its output is only sound if all the statements (premises) in the program are true

  • Is it easy to check if a program is valid?

    Is it easy to check if a program is sound?

Inductive Logic

  • Seeks to find general principles from premises.

  • Does not work to prove something purely from definitions

  • Requires context (premises must align with reality).

Discussion

  • P1: If I work hard at university I’ll get a good grade
  • P2: If I get a good grade I’ll get a good job
  • Con: If I work hard at university, then I’ll get a good job

Is this good reasoning? Why?

  • For maths nerds:

    • Premises: (If A then B) AND (If B then C)
    • Conclusion: If A then C

    is called transitivity.

Problems

  • P1

    • Inept teachers
    • Focus on the wrong things
    • Subjectivity

  • P2

    • a “good job” may not require a degree at all, employers may view you as overqualified
    • lack of employment opportunities in your area of expertise
    • academically brilliant but lacking employability and commercial awareness

  • P1 + P2

    • competition against more and more people with degrees

Inductive keywords

  • Sound: “correctly” formulated arguments

  • Unsound: arguments contain logical flaws

  • Cogent: arguments are sound and align with reality,

  • Uncogent: premices might be sound, but they do not align with reality.

Checking inductive logic

Problem Solving

  • You may have been told

    “Programming is all about problem solving.”

  • Break the problem down into small, easy to manage steps.

  • These steps can be combined into a solution for a problem.

Thinking about thinking

  • “Meta”: beyond or self-referencing

  • “Cognition”: the acquisition of knowledge and understanding through thought, experience, and senses

  • “Metacognition”: exploring the way we acquire knowledge and understanding.

  • Assisting us in applying that knowledge.

  • Metacognition in philosophy typically involves

    • Ontology: theories of being and

    • Epistemology: theories of knowledge,

      but Educational Psychologists prefer the word metacognition

The Dunning–Kruger effect

Perception vs reality

Perceived performance does not accurately reflect actual performance

Low-performing people tend to over-estimate, higher-performing people tend to under-estimate.

“We often think we’re better than we are”, but we can also be conditioned.

Three levels of problem solving

  1. Application
  • able to apply a structured set of problem solving tools
  1. Understanding

  • knowing Why certain techniques are used,

  • able to improve upon the basic set of tools.

  • Metacognition

    • Able to see the problem from multiple perspectives and select the best tools for the job.
    • Able to design your own bespoke set of problem solving tools.

In the UK, after income tax and national insurance, who has the largest take-home salary?

  • A couple, each of which earns \(21,000\),

  • A single person earning \(40,000\)

  • A single person earning \(46,200\)

Take-home pay

According to [https://www.thesalarycalculator.co.uk]:

  • \(2 \times 21,000 = 37,279.2\)

  • \(1 \times 40,000 = 32,319,60\)

  • $1 ,200 = 36,783.60

We need to ask questions…

  • How does the UK tax system work?
    • the UK has a progressive taxation system
    • and a tax free allowance of £12,570 before tax is paid
    • This means the two individuals both get the tax allowance.
  • What factors affect the tax calculation beyond the basic rate?
    • Pension contributions, taxable benefits, marriage allowance, special tax codes.
  • We can say that \(20,000\times 2 \ne 40,000\) in all cases

What is \(0.1 + 0.2\)?

Floating point problems

  • Computers cannot handle numbers after the decimal point well.

  • Stored using scientific notation using binary.

  • Binary only has \(2\) as a prime factor,

    this is why we Ed likes base \(12 = 1 \cdot 12 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 3 \cdot 4\).

  • See [https://0.30000000000000004.com/]

Summary

  • You can work your butt off at uni, get excellent grades and may still not get a good job at the end of it.
  • Suppose you do get a high-paying job. Then the progressive tax system means you might end up with less take-home pay than othres earning less but in a different situation.
  • Computers cannot even add up properly, so what’s the point in doingn computing in the first place?
  • Don’t dispair, it’s more important to enjoy life and play than do nothing but work anyway!

Which statement is more accurate?

  • A: Bath Spa University is situated around the Bath area, it teaches Computing, Drama, and Advanced Zebra Studies.

  • B: Bath Spa University teaches Computing mainly at its Locksbrook campus. It became a University in August 2005, having been previously known as as Dancing Penguin University College.

  • C: Bath Spa University is a collection of buildings.

  • A: Bath Spa University is situated around the Bath area, it teaches Computing, Drama, and Advanced Zebra Studies.

    • situated around the Bath area
    • it teaches Computing, true
    • [it teaches] Drama, true
    • [it teaches] Advanced Zebra Studies. false

  • B: Bath Spa University teaches Computing mainly at its Locksbrook campus. It became a University in August 2005, having been previously known as as Dancing Penguin University College.

    • teaches Computing true
    • [teaches Computing] mainly at its Locksbrook campus false
    • It became a University in August 2005 true
    • previously known as Dancing Penguin University College. false

  • C: Bath Spa University is a collection of buildings.
    • collection of buildings true
